questions.prompt: Why does returning `NonMovable{42}` from `NonMovable make()` compile in C++17+ even though both its copy and move constructors are `= delete`?
options: Because C++17 ignores = delete inside return statements
Because NonMovable{42} is a prvalue that directly initializes the caller's target slot without materializing or moving a temporary
Because NRVO automatically synthesizes a private move constructor
Because return NonMovable{42} calls memcpy on the stack frame
questions.explanation: Since C++17 ([basic.lval], [dcl.init]), a prvalue is an unmaterialized initializer rather than a temporary object. Initializing a NonMovable destination from a NonMovable prvalue constructs directly in place with zero copy or move calls.

questions.prompt: What is the practical effect of writing `return std::move(s);` when `s` is a local `std::string` inside `std::string build()`?
options: It triggers guaranteed copy elision by converting s into a prvalue
It speeds up the function because plain return s would copy s
It prevents NRVO and forces a move construction instead of zero-cost in-place construction
It causes undefined behavior because s is destroyed before the move finishes
questions.explanation: NRVO applies only when the return operand is the plain name of a local automatic variable. std::move(s) turns it into a function call xvalue, disabling NRVO and forcing a move constructor (-Wpessimizing-move).

questions.prompt: In C++23, which snippet fails to compile when `Token` has deleted copy and move constructors?
options: Token a = Token{1};
Token make() { return Token{2}; } Token b = make();
Token bad() { Token t{3}; return t; }
void f(Token); f(Token{4});
questions.explanation: Returning a named local variable t relies on optional NRVO, not guaranteed prvalue elision. Because NRVO is optional under [class.copy.elision], the language still requires an accessible copy or move constructor for t.

questions.prompt: Given `std::string passthrough(std::string param) { return param; }`, what happens in the `return param;` statement?
options: Mandatory prvalue elision constructs param directly in the caller's return slot
NRVO applies because param is a named variable inside passthrough
Copy constructor runs because param is an lvalue
NRVO is forbidden on function parameters, so implicit move invokes std::string(std::string&&)
questions.explanation: Under [class.copy.elision], NRVO excludes function parameters because parameter storage lives in the caller/ABI frame. However, param is move-eligible, so implicit move constructs the return object using std::string's move constructor.

questions.prompt: Suppose `Derived` publicly inherits from `Base` and `Derived make_derived();` returns a prvalue. Does `Base b = make_derived();` bypass `Base`'s move constructor via mandatory copy elision?
options: No; mandatory prvalue elision requires the prvalue's cv-unqualified type to match Base, so make_derived() materializes and fails because Base(Base&&) is deleted
Yes; mandatory elision constructs only the Base subobject directly in b
Yes, provided Derived adds no data members
No; it invokes reinterpret_cast<Base&&>(make_derived())
questions.explanation: [dcl.init] grants direct initialization without temporary materialization only when the prvalue has the same cv-unqualified class type as the destination object. When constructing Base from a Derived prvalue, Derived materializes via [conv.rval] and Base's deleted move constructor makes the initialization ill-formed.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `x = make_widget();` (copy assignment to an already-constructed `Widget x`) is accurate under C++23?
options: Mandatory copy elision constructs the return value of make_widget() directly on top of x without calling operator=
make_widget() undergoes temporary materialization conversion ([conv.rval]) to an xvalue, and Widget::operator=(Widget&&) (or const Widget&) is called
x is automatically destroyed and placement-newed via NRVO
Assignment to an existing object is ill-formed if make_widget() returns a prvalue
questions.explanation: Mandatory prvalue elision applies only to initialization of a new object, never assignment to an existing object. Because operator= takes a reference parameter, temporary materialization ([conv.rval]) creates a temporary xvalue bound to operator='s parameter.
